rmt-2010-power-01a.title: A tree
rmt-2010-power-01a.body:
A connected graph with $8$ vertices and $7$ edges is a tree (no cycles); any tree works. Take the path $v_1-v_2-\dots-v_8$ and colour its seven edges in turn red, blue, green, red, blue, green, red. It is connected, simple, has $8$ vertices and $7$ edges, and uses $3$ colours.

**Answer: e.g. the path above (any tree with a $3$-colouring of its edges is acceptable)**

rmt-2010-power-01b.title: Pentagon and pentagram
rmt-2010-power-01b.body:
Place the vertices $0,1,2,3,4$ around a pentagon. Colour the five sides (pairs at difference $\pm1\pmod5$) blue and the five diagonals (pairs at difference $\pm2$) red.

A blue triangle would be three vertices pairwise adjacent on the pentagon, but the sides form a single $5$-cycle, which has no triangle. The red diagonals form the pentagram, also a $5$-cycle ($0-2-4-1-3-0$), which has no triangle either. So there is no monochromatic triangle.

**Answer: sides blue, diagonals red**

rmt-2010-power-02.title: Pigeonhole at a vertex
rmt-2010-power-02.body: Pick a vertex $v$. It has $5$ edges, each red or blue, so at least $3$ have the same colour; say $v$ is joined by blue edges to $a,b,c$ (the other case is symmetric with the colours swapped). Look at the three edges $ab,bc,ca$. If any of them is blue, say $ab$, then $v,a,b$ form a blue triangle. If none is blue, all three are red and $a,b,c$ form a red triangle. Either way there is a monochromatic triangle. ∎

rmt-2010-power-03a.title: Explicit colouring
rmt-2010-power-03a.body:
Label the vertices of $K_8$ by $\mathbb Z_8$. Colour the edge $ij$ **red** if $i-j\equiv\pm1$ or $4\pmod8$ (the $8$-cycle plus the four long diagonals) and **blue** if $i-j\equiv\pm2$ or $\pm3$.

*No red triangle.* A triangle $i,j,k$ would need $j-i$, $k-j$ and $k-i=(j-i)+(k-j)$ all in $\{1,-1,4\}$. The possible sums of two elements of $\{1,-1,4\}$ are $2,0,5,-2,3,0\pmod8$, and none of them is $\pm1$ or $4$. So there is no red triangle.

*No blue $K_4$.* A blue $K_4$ is $4$ vertices with no two at red difference (i.e. no two adjacent on the $8$-cycle and no two antipodal). Pair up the antipodal vertices $\{r,r+4\}$, $r=0,1,2,3$. Four vertices with no antipodal pair contain exactly one from each pair: $x_r\in\{r,r+4\}$. Put $b_r=0$ if $x_r=r$ and $b_r=1$ if $x_r=r+4$. For $r=0,1,2$ the vertices $x_r,x_{r+1}$ are adjacent on the cycle exactly when $b_r=b_{r+1}$ (e.g. $x_0=0,x_1=1$ or $x_0=4,x_1=5$), so we need $b_0\ne b_1\ne b_2\ne b_3$, forcing $b_3\ne b_0$. But $x_3,x_0$ are adjacent exactly when $b_3\ne b_0$ ($x_3=7,x_0=0$ or $x_3=3,x_0=4$), a contradiction. So there is no blue $K_4$.

Hence $K_8$ has a colouring with no red $K_3$ and no blue $K_4$, so $R(3,4)>8$. ∎

rmt-2010-power-03b.title: Upper bound by counting degrees
rmt-2010-power-03b.body:
*$R(4,3)\le9$.* Suppose $K_9$ is coloured with no red $K_4$ and no blue triangle.

- A vertex $v$ has at most $5$ red edges: if it had $6$, the six red neighbours would form a $K_6$, which by Problem 2 contains a monochromatic triangle; a blue one is forbidden, a red one together with $v$ gives a red $K_4$.
- A vertex has at most $3$ blue edges: if it had $4$ blue neighbours, any blue edge among them gives a blue triangle with $v$, so all $6$ edges among them are red, giving a red $K_4$.

Each vertex has $8$ edges, so it has exactly $5$ red and $3$ blue edges. Then the number of blue edge-ends is $9\cdot3=27$, which is odd; but it equals twice the number of blue edges, a contradiction. So every colouring of $K_9$ has a red $K_4$ or a blue $K_3$.

*$R(4,3)>8$.* Take the colouring of $K_8$ from the previous problem (no red $K_3$, no blue $K_4$) and swap the two colours: it has no blue $K_3$ and no red $K_4$.

Therefore $R(4,3)=9$. ∎

rmt-2010-power-04a.title: Proof
rmt-2010-power-04a.body:
Let $N=R(n,m-1)+R(n-1,m)$ and colour the edges of $K_N$ red and blue. Pick a vertex $v$; it has $N-1=R(n,m-1)+R(n-1,m)-1$ edges. If $v$ had at most $R(n-1,m)-1$ red edges and at most $R(n,m-1)-1$ blue edges, it would have at most $N-2$ edges; so it has either at least $R(n-1,m)$ red edges or at least $R(n,m-1)$ blue edges.

*Case 1: at least $R(n-1,m)$ red edges.* Let $W$ be the set of vertices joined to $v$ by red edges. By the definition of $R(n-1,m)$, $W$ contains a red $K_{n-1}$ or a blue $K_m$. A red $K_{n-1}$ together with $v$ is a red $K_n$.

*Case 2: at least $R(n,m-1)$ blue edges.* Let $W'$ be the blue neighbours of $v$. It contains a red $K_n$ or a blue $K_{m-1}$, and a blue $K_{m-1}$ together with $v$ is a blue $K_m$.

In both cases the colouring contains a red $K_n$ or a blue $K_m$, so $R(n,m)\le N$. ∎

rmt-2010-power-04b.title: Induction on $n+m$
rmt-2010-power-04b.body:
*Base cases.* $R(2,m)=m$: in any red/blue colouring of $K_m$ either some edge is red (a red $K_2$) or all edges are blue (a blue $K_m$), while $K_{m-1}$ coloured entirely blue has neither. Similarly $R(n,2)=n$.

*Induction step.* Let $n,m\ge3$ and suppose $R(n,m-1)$ and $R(n-1,m)$ exist (they have smaller $n+m$). The argument of part (a) shows that every red/blue colouring of $K_N$ with $N=R(n,m-1)+R(n-1,m)$ contains a red $K_n$ or a blue $K_m$ (it uses only that the two numbers on the right exist). So there is such an $N$, and the least one, $R(n,m)$, exists. ∎

rmt-2010-power-05a.title: Pigeonhole
rmt-2010-power-05a.body: Take $n+1$ of the points. There are only $n$ rows, so two of the points lie in the same row, and the edge between them is blue. A single row contains only $n$ points, so the $n+1$ points cannot all lie in one row: two of them are in different rows, and the edge between them is red. ∎

rmt-2010-power-05b.title: Conclusion
rmt-2010-power-05b.body: In this colouring of $K_{n^2}$ no $K_{n+1}$ is monochromatic (each contains a red and a blue edge). So $K_{n^2}$ has a colouring with neither a red $K_{n+1}$ nor a blue $K_{n+1}$, which means $R(n+1,n+1)>n^2$. ∎

rmt-2010-power-06a.title: Union bound
rmt-2010-power-06a.body: Fix a set of $n$ vertices. It has $\binom n2$ edges, and it is monochromatic if all are red (probability $2^{-\binom n2}$) or all are blue (probability $2^{-\binom n2}$): total $2^{1-\binom n2}$. There are $\binom mn$ choices of the set, and the probability that at least one of them is monochromatic is at most the sum of the individual probabilities (union bound), i.e. at most $\binom mn2^{1-\binom n2}$. ∎

rmt-2010-power-06b.title: Multiply the inequality
rmt-2010-power-06b.body: Multiplying $\binom mn<2^{\binom n2-1}$ by $2^{1-\binom n2}>0$ gives $\binom mn2^{1-\binom n2}<1$. By the previous problem the probability of a monochromatic $K_n$ is at most this quantity, hence less than $1$. ∎

rmt-2010-power-06c.title: Compute $m^n$
rmt-2010-power-06c.body:
$m^n=2^{n\left(\frac n2-\frac1n-\frac12\right)}=2^{\frac{n^2-n}2-1}=2^{\binom n2-1}$. With $\binom mn<m^n$ this gives $\binom mn<2^{\binom n2-1}$. (The printed statement has the exponent as $1-\binom n2$; the inequality needed for the previous part is $\binom mn<2^{\binom n2-1}$, which is what the computation shows.)

**Conclusion.** Let $m'=\lfloor m\rfloor$ (the number of vertices must be an integer). If $m'<n$, then $R(n,n)\ge n>m$ trivially. Otherwise $\binom{m'}n<m'^n\le m^n=2^{\binom n2-1}$, so by the previous two parts a random colouring of $K_{m'}$ has positive probability of containing no monochromatic $K_n$; hence some colouring of $K_{m'}$ has none, and $R(n,n)>m'$. Since $R(n,n)$ is an integer and $m'+1>m$, we get $R(n,n)\ge m'+1>m=2^{\frac n2-\frac1n-\frac12}$. ∎

rmt-2010-power-07.title: Flagging argument
rmt-2010-power-07.body:
Take any red/blue colouring of $K_N$ with $N=4^n=2^{2n}$. Build vertices $v_1,v_2,\dots,v_{2n}$ and sets $T_0\supset T_1\supset\dots$ as follows. Start with $T_0=$ all vertices, $|T_0|=2^{2n}$. At step $k$ ($k=1,\dots,2n$), $T_{k-1}$ has at least $2^{2n-k+1}$ vertices. Choose any $v_k\in T_{k-1}$. The other at least $2^{2n-k+1}-1$ vertices of $T_{k-1}$ are joined to $v_k$ by red or blue edges, so at least $\left\lceil\frac{2^{2n-k+1}-1}2\right\rceil=2^{2n-k}$ of them are joined by edges of the same colour $c_k$. Let $T_k$ be that set of at least $2^{2n-k}$ vertices, and give $v_k$ the flag $c_k$.

For $i<j$ we have $v_j\in T_{j-1}\subseteq T_i$, so the edge $v_iv_j$ has colour $c_i$ (the colour of the flag of the earlier vertex). Among the $2n$ flags, by pigeonhole at least $n$ have the same colour $c$. The corresponding vertices $v_{i_1},\dots,v_{i_n}$ satisfy: every edge $v_{i_a}v_{i_b}$ ($a<b$) has colour $c_{i_a}=c$. So they form a monochromatic $K_n$. Hence $R(n,n)\le4^n$. ∎

rmt-2010-power-08.title: Pigeonhole and $R(3,3)=6$
rmt-2010-power-08.body: Take a $3$-colouring of $K_{17}$ and a vertex $v$. It has $16$ edges in $3$ colours, and $\frac{16}3>5$, so some colour, say green, appears on at least $6$ edges at $v$. Let $W$ be the set of at least $6$ vertices at the other ends of these green edges. If some edge inside $W$ is green, it forms a green triangle with $v$. Otherwise the edges inside $W$ use only red and blue, and since $|W|\ge6=R(3,3)$ (Problem 2), $W$ contains a red or a blue triangle. In every case there is a monochromatic triangle, so $R(3,3,3)\le17$. ∎

rmt-2010-power-09.title: Merging two colours
rmt-2010-power-09.body:
Let $m=R\big(n_1,\dots,n_{k-2},R(n_k,n_{k-1})\big)$, a $(k-1)$-colour Ramsey number (we may assume it exists, by induction on $k$, starting from the two-colour numbers whose existence was shown in Problem 4). Take any $k$-colouring of the edges of $K_m$ with colours $c_1,\dots,c_k$. Re-colour every edge of colour $c_k$ with colour $c_{k-1}$; this is a $(k-1)$-colouring. By the definition of $m$, either there is a $K_{n_i}$ of colour $c_i$ for some $i\le k-2$ (it was already of colour $c_i$ in the original colouring, and we are done), or there is a $K_{R(n_k,n_{k-1})}$ all of whose edges have the merged colour. In the original colouring each of its edges has colour $c_{k-1}$ or $c_k$, so by the definition of $R(n_{k-1},n_k)$ it contains a $K_{n_{k-1}}$ of colour $c_{k-1}$ or a $K_{n_k}$ of colour $c_k$. In every case the original colouring has the required monochromatic clique, so $R(n_1,\dots,n_k)\le m$. ∎

Induction on $k$ then shows that $R(n_1,\dots,n_k)$ exists for all $n_1,\dots,n_k$.

rmt-2010-power-10a.title: Induction on $r$
rmt-2010-power-10a.body: For $r=1$: $R_1=3=3\cdot1!$. Suppose $r\ge2$ and that every $(r-1)$-colouring of $K_{3(r-1)!}$ contains a monochromatic triangle. Take an $r$-colouring of $K_N$ with $N=3\cdot r!$ and a vertex $v$. It has $3\cdot r!-1=r\cdot3(r-1)!-1$ edges in $r$ colours, so some colour $c$ appears on at least $\left\lceil\frac{r\cdot3(r-1)!-1}r\right\rceil=3(r-1)!$ of them. Let $W$ be the set of vertices joined to $v$ by edges of colour $c$, $|W|\ge3(r-1)!$. If an edge inside $W$ has colour $c$, it forms a triangle of colour $c$ with $v$. Otherwise no edge inside $W$ has colour $c$: $W$ is coloured with only $r-1$ colours and has at least $3(r-1)!$ vertices, so by the induction hypothesis it contains a monochromatic triangle. Hence $R_r\le3\cdot r!$. ∎

rmt-2010-power-10b.title: Doubling construction
rmt-2010-power-10b.body:
We show by induction on $r$ that there is an $r$-colouring of $K_{2^r}$ without a monochromatic triangle, which gives $R_r>2^r$.

For $r=1$: $K_2$ with one colour has only one edge, so no triangle.

Step: suppose $K_{2^{r-1}}$ has an $(r-1)$-colouring with no monochromatic triangle. Take two disjoint copies of it (together $2^r$ vertices) and colour every edge between the two copies with the new colour $r$. A triangle with all three vertices in one copy is not monochromatic by hypothesis. A triangle with vertices in both copies has two vertices in one copy and one in the other, so two of its edges are cross edges of colour $r$ and the third is an edge inside a copy, which has a colour different from $r$; it is not monochromatic. So the new colouring of $K_{2^r}$ has no monochromatic triangle, and $R_r>2^r$. ∎

rmt-2010-power-11.title: Infinite flagging argument
rmt-2010-power-11.body:
Put $T_0=V$. Given an infinite set $T_{k-1}$, let $v_k$ be its least element. The infinitely many edges from $v_k$ to the other elements of $T_{k-1}$ are red or blue, so infinitely many have the same colour $c_k$; let $T_k$ be the infinite set of those other endpoints. Repeat forever. This produces vertices $v_1<v_2<\dots$ and colours $c_1,c_2,\dots$ with the property: for $i<j$, $v_j\in T_{j-1}\subseteq T_i$, so the edge $v_iv_j$ has colour $c_i$.

Since each $c_i$ is red or blue, one of the colours, say $c$, occurs for infinitely many indices $i_1<i_2<\dots$. Let $V'=\{v_{i_1},v_{i_2},\dots\}$, an infinite set. For $a<b$ the edge $v_{i_a}v_{i_b}$ has colour $c_{i_a}=c$. So all edges between points of $V'$ have the same colour. ∎
